January 28, 2025

Senator Talbot Ross, Representative Pluecker, and members of the Joint Standing Committee on
Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry, I am Craig Lapine, Director of the Bureau of
Agriculture, Food and Rural Resources in the Department of Agriculture, Conservation and
Forestry (DACF). I am here today to speak in support of LD 40, An Act to Make Changes to the
Commercial Large Game Shooting Area (CLGSA) License Transfer Process.
A Commercial Large Game Shooting Area is an enclosed space where large game are kept and
customers pay a fee to hunt these animals. CLGSAs are stocked with specific, permitted, non-
native species, primarily four members of the deer family: red deer, elk, sika, and fallow deer.
These non-native cervids are bred on Maine deer farms, with both CLGSAs and deer farms regulated tln'ough DACF's captive cervid program.
This bill would amend the statute governing CLGSA license transfers. It would grant the
Commissioner final authority to approve license transfers when applicants meet statutory
requirements.
Under current law, license holders must notify the Commissioner 30 days before a transfer, providing the transfer date and the recipient's name, mailing address, and telephone number. This notification does not give the Department any authority or active oversight role to ensure a viable
transfer/sale or a license before it occurs.
Maine statute has a maximum of 11 CLGSA facilities, and license transfers occur infrequently.
However, the law currently does not require any verification from the Department that new
license holders meet the requirements and obligations outlined in subsection 2 of the statute before such a license transfer takes place, which has caused challenges. Specifically, an
individual purchased a CLGSA facility in a private transaction in 2023, and although the existing
30-day license notification standard was met, the new owner was unprepared and unable to meet the requirements of the license. This meant that when the license expired, the purchaser Was

Senator Talbot-Ross, Representative Pluecker and esteemed members of the Agriculture,
Conservation and Forestry committee thank you for hearing my testimony today. First, I want to highlight that I am the reason you are hearing this bill, as written, here today. You see, I purchased a CLGSA permit last year with the hopes of someday operating one of these facilities. I am sure the department has their own version of what happened, and they can share it with youbut I am going to share it from my view. Originally, I asked if it was possible to buy the permit and the land and build a facility. The department told me yes, that was alright as long as I had an address to attach the permit to. When it came time to for me to renew the license, they had new legal guidance that what they had told me was wrong, that I needed to have an inspectable fence, which I did not have. So they suggested that just to appease the law, I attach my permit to one of the fenced areas at my friends farm. I re-applied and was again denied because at that location it
was too close to another permit. Keep in mind, I was making no physical changes to the facility, it would operate just as it had- I was only trying to keep possession of the permit I paid $30,000 for. To summarize, so I can talk about what I want to talk about, the department moved the goal
post a number of times, ultimately making it impossible for me to retain the permit resulting in a financial loss of $30,000. Now, instead of fixing those issues that stopped me from keeping my
permit, they want to give the commissioner a veto over permit sales. That is not an appropriate solution to the problem.
What is an appropriate solution is the amendment before you, to create a stakeholder group to
address the outdated and arbitrary nature of CLGSA regulations. When this program was
originally regulated it was designed to kill the program over time, a slow death of regulatory hoops for permit holders to jump through with the stated end goal of not having these facilities
anymore. I am asking you to change that today. I am asking you to change the attitude of
loathing this program, to one of promoting it. You see, these facilities, other than the means of harvesting their livestock, are just farms. They are farms that allow a heightened level of involvement by their customer. They allow customers to come to the facility, choose the animal to harvest, see the process the entire way through from field to fork. Everyone doesn't have the ability to successfully deer hunt, or bear hunt. Or maybe they do, but it does not provide enough
meat for them. Take me for example, I harvested a Red Stag this fall to supplement the meat I got
from 2 whitetail, a bear and half of a Moose. It sounds like a lot, but I eat about 2lbs of game
meat a day so it goes quickly. These programs allow folks to be as close to their farmed food as possible and they need to be protected and promoted. Please, allow the permit holders a venue
with the department to make long-needed changes to this program for the betterment of the farmers and farmed animals. I would happily answer any questions you may have.

Committee on Agriculture, Conservation, and Forestry, thank you so much for the
opportunity for me to present LD 40, An Act to Make Changes to the Commercial Large
Game Shooting Area (CLGSA) License Transfer Process. This is the Department's bill so
I will only speak briefly to the bill before giving the hearing over to them to discuss the
bill in greater detail.
A Commercial Large Game Shooting Area (CLGSA) is an enclosed space where
customers pay to hunt non-native deer species. Both CLGSAs and deer farms are
regulated by the DACF's captive cervid program.
This bill amends the statute governing CLGSA license transfers, giving the
Commissioner final authority to approve transfers once applicants meet statutory requirements. Currently, license holders only need to notify the Commissioner 30 days
before a transfer, but there's no oversight to ensure the new owner meets all
requirements before the transfer. This has led to issues, such as a 2023 transfer where
the new owner was unable to meet licensing requirements within the statutorily
defined timeframe.
The proposed amendment would add a verification step, ensuring that buyers meet all
necessary licensing requirements before completing a transfer.
Thank you for your time.
